summary:
FieldMate is support decision system forcrop rotation for farmers.
Vietnam has a strong agriculturalal foundation. yet Vietnamese farmers still face many challenges including cimate change, water management , resources. etc. Addressing this problem, our team introduces FieldMate to fill the gap of the market.
details:
The problem: the calendar farmers trusted no longer works

For a smallholder family, the farming year used to follow a known rhythm. Now heat, drought and off-season rain shift it from one year to the next, and in coastal deltas salt water creeps up the canals earlier. A wrong call on when to water or what to plant next can cost a whole crop. We built our demo in Vietnam's Mekong Delta, where all of this happens at once. Satellite data that could warn them already exists, but it lives in formats, websites and jargon that a 60-year-old farmer with a basic smartphone will never open. Most farm apps also expect people to type things in: dates, inputs, yields. Our users won't, and shouldn't have to.

What FieldMate does

1. Set up in one minute, then almost no typing. The farmer drags a box over their field on a satellite map. FieldMate recognizes the crop group (paddy rice, upland crops, orchard, water or bare soil) and estimates the sowing date from satellite imagery (NASA HLS and OPERA radar). For our demo field, that is "Rice field found, sown Oct 3".

2. A daily companion, not a dashboard. A season progress bar shows where the crop is. When the data says something needs doing, a task appears with the reason and its source. Task rules already cover rice, mung bean and corn; on the demo rice field, the season looks like this:

Drain the field 5–7 days: day 30, rice is tillering (HLS sowing date + POWER heat units)

Let water into the field: 20 mm short over 7 days, soil 16% drier than normal (POWER + SMAP)

Store fresh water: canal salinity rising (salinity station)

Brown spot risk: hot and humid 2 days, about 40 mm of rain in the next 3 days (POWER). Tapping the alert opens a disease card with a photo, what it looks like, what to do now, and when to call the plant-protection officer.

The farmer taps one option. It is logged on a Season map, and the next satellite pass checks whether the work actually happened.

3. The next-season decision, three weeks before harvest. FieldMate builds three rotation plans from a crop catalog (rice, mung bean, corn, vegetables such as cucumber, or a fallow rest), a transition table and a scoring engine: A is always the current practice. For our test field in the 2019–2020 drought-and-salt year, the plans were: A, rice as usual (12/100); B, rest the field with straw mulch (86/100); C, mung bean then back to rice (54/100). Each plan shows water need, salt limit, nitrogen left for the soil and reference profit, plus a "Why?" in plain language. Farmers can move priority sliders, or tap "Auto-tune to my field" to let the field's own data set them. Before a plan is shown, code checks it against 6 hard rules: the crop is in the catalog, the crop switch is allowed, dates fall in the planting window, every number matches the data, plan A is the current practice, and every reason is tied to a real index.

4. A soil ledger built from the satellite archive. FieldMate counts past seasons from HLS greenness (our field had 8 rice seasons in a row) and turns that into a soil-rest argument the farmer can see.

How NASA data makes it possible

NASA POWER: daily temperature, humidity and rain for heat units, crop stage, water deficit and disease risk; also the 10-year "normal" that every "compared with usual" line is made against.

SMAP L4 (SPL4SMGP): soil moisture compared with previous years.

HLS (Landsat + Sentinel-2, 30 m) and HLS vegetation indices: crop greenness, sowing date, crop type and the history of past seasons.

OPERA RTC-S1 radar: sees water on the field through monsoon clouds, so FieldMate can still confirm "drained" or "flooded" in the rainy season.

ECOSTRESS (ESI): water stress confirmation for dry-season upland crops.

MODIS (MOD13Q1, MOD16A2GF): fills cloud gaps in greenness and adds evapotranspiration.

Local sources sit on top: weekly pest bulletins from Vietnam's Plant Protection Department, an agronomy rotation table based on FAO-56 and provincial guidance, and canal salinity readings in the format of the Mekong Rynan IoT network. In this demo the salinity readings are simulated, because we have no data agreement with the network yet. The app labels them that way.

What makes it different

"Do nothing" can be the right answer. Most tools push farmers to plant more. FieldMate can recommend resting the field when water and salt say so, and show what that saves.

The satellite is the witness, not the farmer. Because satellites verify the work, FieldMate quietly builds a farm diary nobody had to write. Down the line, that same diary can support VietGAP traceability, crop-insurance claims or a loan application.

Explainable by design. No language model writes the advice. Plans come from rules, tables and scores we can show line by line, and every number has a confidence level.

Tested against the past, honestly. Our demo replays a full year, Sep 2019 to Aug 2020, one day at a time. On each day the app only sees data available up to that day, and forecasts as they were issued that day.

How we built it

App: Flutter (Dart) for web and Android from one codebase, Riverpod, SQLite. The Android build adds local notifications, a home-screen widget (Jetpack Glance) and background updates (WorkManager). The web version runs fully in the browser, with no login and no data sent anywhere.

Data pipeline: Python with earthaccess, rasterio and numpy, pulling from NASA POWER, AppEEARS, the ASF archive and Earthdata.

Hosting: Firebase Hosting for the web demo.

Demo video: built with Remotion, with every interface element recreated from the real app. All music and sound effects were synthesized in code.

What we considered

Small fields, big pixels. Our field is 0.27 ha, smaller than many satellite pixels. When data is regional (SMAP 9 km, POWER ~50 km), the app says so instead of pretending it is field-level.

Clouds. Optical imagery disappears in the rainy season, so radar (OPERA RTC-S1) carries the water signal.

Data that looked useful but wasn't. We tested NASADEM to spot low-lying fields, then dropped it: its meter-level error is larger than the 15–30 cm that separates high and low fields in the delta. The field's flood history from radar and HLS does that job better.

Literacy and trust. Plain words, icons, large text, a confidence dot next to every number, and a nudge to call a local expert where data runs out.

Honesty. Agronomic thresholds that are not yet validated by a local expert are marked as unverified in our knowledge base. Simulated inputs are labeled.

What's next

The engine is not tied to rice or to one delta: crops are data files, and the NASA layers are global. Next steps are more crop profiles and disease libraries, more regions, real-time salinity from local stations, a "send to extension officer" button, and NASA's NISAR L-band radar for seeing under dense crop canopy.
